I knew that it was Mladic because I recognised him but also because we had been told that he would come." My question is this: Who had told you that General Mladic would come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me quote your statement further: "I was some 10 to 15 metres away from him when he gave a speech standing by the side of the pitch. He spoke without a megaphone, just normally, as it was very quiet. He stated that he was General Mladic and that we would all be exchanged. And that there were hundreds of Serb lines between here -- between us and Tuzla and that not even a bird could get through the lines. He said we would be organised into groups to collect all the bodies from the hills and then we would be taken to Bratunac to have lunch there," and so on and so forth, and then that you would be taken for an exchange. End of quote. So this is something that you mention in your statement. Is what I've read out consistent with what you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, after all these years, can you actually remember whether it was indeed General Mladic who came there and whether he addressed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: I think so. I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this reflect the actual events? In line 6, after this paragraph, there is an indication there where it says: "And then he elected five of his men to compile lists of our names, first and last names. This took about an hour." Now, my question is this: Was a roster actually made, was a list compiled while you were waiting on that soccer pitch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did all of this indicate that you would indeed be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Well, that's what we thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a camera filming this, your assemblage there at the football pitch and the address by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Later on, were you taken in the direction which Mladic had mentioned in his speech? Were you taken to Potocari for lunch and -- to Bratunac for lunch and then on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately we were taken to Bratunac but we weren't given any lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Unfortunately or, rather, you did not speak about this at length in the other statement but you did arrive in the end --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request: Could the accused please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters didn't catch the whole of the last question. Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was whether you had actually arrived in Batkovic, as Mladic had indicated, where then you were exchanged in December 1995, could you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Well, I did manage to get there because I managed to escape the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is now on record and I will now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, on the way to Bratunac, did the soldiers still keep telling you that you would be exchanged once you got to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it possible that someone had actually changed the order issued by the chief -- by the Commander-in-Chief, and that you would be exchanged once you reached Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were only exchanged in December of that year and we know what you went through. Could you now tell us, please, something about a question that was put to you by the Prosecutor? He questioned you at length about your detention at Batkovic. Would you please tell us: Were you registered by the ICRS as soon as you arrived at Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this organised by the prison authorities who held you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, do you know who it is who can organise the way work is being done and the way the prisoners are treated at a detention facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why you were taken to these sites that you had survived? As you said, the execution sites. And you mentioned the areas that were completely voided of Muslim populations, where everyone had fled. And why then were you taken to the areas that were settled, where there were also UNPROFOR members and so on? So can you tell us, have you given that any consideration? Why would that be done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Well, I think you are better placed to know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, thank you, but I keep wondering why you were taken through all this whole ordeal, taken to Zvornik and so on, where you would have to actually go through crossroads where there were in place all these international -- members of the international community and so on, while they could take you to other places where you could be accommodated and exchanged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you a few questions about one of your statements, or testimonies. What would you prefer, that I put these questions to you in open session or in private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask you about a trial that wasn't conducted before this Tribunal but in another country. Now, I don't want to go into further details. Perhaps the Prosecutor can tell us and assist you with whether it should be in open session or in private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we should go into private session, referring to -- I'm referring to the discussion we had yesterday. Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's exactly the position of the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We turn to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, on page 56, lines 15 to 16, you said, as the witness stated, that he didn't know the answers to the questions that are put to him. I don't think that this is a correct comment. He didn't know many answers to many of your questions, but he answered some of your questions. Just to make it a little bit more specific. The document 1D556 will be received under seal. I misspoke again. 566, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 65 ter number 1D566 shall be admitted into evidence and assigned Exhibit D154 under seal, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, that should be under seal because there would be a link to the name of the witness. The document 1D373, I would like to ask the Defence, Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering that as well? This is not a statement of this witness but a different document you used with the witness. Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, we move for this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification pending translation. Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to say why I said what I said, if you permit me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are dealing with the document. You may do it a moment later. 1D373 will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 1D373 shall be assigned Exhibit D155, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. A moment ago you commented on what I just said. To my last question, page 56, line 3, the witness answered: "I know nothing about this." And then I said that I was not going to ask him anything more simply because he said that he didn't know anything more about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I take it that that was perhaps a problem of interpretation. The singular and the plural, the question and the questions. I think we have clarified the situation. Yes. I'm reminded that there is another document, 1D561. What about this? Yes, you were tendering that as well? I see that should be admitted and will be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a document from the Prosecution, so we do not move to have it admitted, and we also did not use it during the cross-examination. So we do not move for it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a clear position. Mr. Elderkin, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Briefly, yes, and certainly I'll be finished before quarter past the hour, if I may. Could I go into private session at the beginning, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd ask to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, General Tolimir has represented in his questioning on, I think, around page 52 and onwards, that there were reasons why the Bosnian Serbs who had captured you would not want to take you up to Zvornik if they wanted to execute the men they had captured. In fact, your answer just now, you referred to the fact that there were international personnel including, for example the DutchBat peacekeepers, perhaps other NGOs present around the Bratunac area but not around the Zvornik area. Does that correctly represent your understanding of where there were international personnel around the time you were captured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: I understood that he asked me whether they were in Srebrenica. That's the question that I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: After the time you were captured on the 13th of July, was your treatment by the Bosnian Serb soldiers who had captured you such that they were treating you in a way where you expected to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a little additional detail. Were you provided food at any point after your capture, before you were taken from Nova Kasaba to Bratunac, then to Pilica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Once, in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And were you provided with sufficient water throughout those three days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were the conditions in which you were kept from the time of your capture until the 16th of July humane conditions in your view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your prior testimony, you referred to the list of names being prepared while General Mladic was present at Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July. Apart from that time when your name was taken, were you interviewed during the time of your capture until the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was your name taken on any other occasion during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: No, not until the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you said that the Red Cross registered you on arrival at the camp. Had you been registered by the Red Cross at any time from your capture on the 13th of July until you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Elderkin. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just wonder if you can clarify some detail for me. From the time when you were captured up to the time when you surrendered to the Red Cross, how long were you in incarceration or in detention or in prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: You are talking about the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'm talking about from the time when you were captured up to the time when you surrendered to the Red Cross, I don't know whether it was at the camp or another type of place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Yes. It was from the 13th to the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-016
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination. You are now free to return to your normal activities and your home. The Chamber would like to thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again and to help us finding out the truth. Thank you very much and the court usher will assist you to leave the courtroom. But, please, wait a moment, stay there. We will leave the courtroom first and then your security will be acknowledged. Thank you very much again. We break now and resume -- do you want to have the floor, Mr. Elderkin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: A matter of seconds, simply the question about P252 from the beginning of the day, that should, indeed, please be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: P, I understand P252. It was referred to as an intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that should be under seal. Thank you very much. We break now and the Chamber will resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. As you know, our president Judge Fluegge cannot be with us for this session. So according to Rule 15 bis, the Trial Chamber can have this hearing according to the rule. I will have the privilege of chairing this last session. Madam Prosecutor, is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The next witness is ready. And just -- this witness will be requiring a Rule 90(E) caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the Trial Chamber had decided to hear this witness as a viva voce witness and not turn him into a 92 bis witness; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct. He will be -- he is a viva voce witness given the Chamber's ruling on that, but what I was referring to was a Rule 90 caution in the event he gets asked a question that is -- that may incriminate, may be incriminating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understood that perfectly. I also know that this witness had not been granted any protective measures. Is that the case? No pseudonym, no voice distortion or face distortion; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This matter came up just recently. It seems that the Registry record didn't show that there were any protective measures, but the last time he testified in Popovic, right before he testified, there was an oral decision that he be granted face distortion. And that -- I can give you the reference for that decision. That was in page 14616 of the Popovic case, on the 3rd of September 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, if I understood you correctly, you would like these measures to be maintained by this Trial Chamber, is that it? You want the same protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, is that given the order of the Court in Popovic, the measures still apply to this witness. The witness has indicated that he still wants these measures in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. The Trial Chamber is satisfied and the measures will be granted. I'm asking the Registry first to move into private session and then to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. Once again, good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to show to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal provide for a number of rights as far as witnesses are concerned. And in your case, I wish to read out loud Rule 90(E) of our rules which might be useful for you. "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent Prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Have you understood this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have. I'm not a lawyer myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Madam Prosecutor has questions to put to you, for her examination-in-chief, and then the floor will be to the Defence, given to the Defence. Ms. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, just as a preliminary matter, we are working with three languages in this courtroom, so I'm going to try to speak very slowly and I'd ask that you speak slowly too and wait before -- wait between me asking the question and you answering the question so that the interpreters can do their job. And if I ask you any question that you don't understand, please let me know and I will do my best to rephrase it so that you do understand it. As you know, my name is Abeer Hasan, and I will proceed with my questions. For the record, what is your name?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: My name is Mile Simanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what is your place and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: 9th of April 1956, the village of Gacici, Sekovici municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us where you resided in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: In 1995, I used to live in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, sir, what do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I'm still a civil engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And could you briefly tell us about the education you received?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: You mean how I received it? During my whole education?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No. If you could tell us the degrees you received.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I'm a civil engineer. I work in this profession for a number of years. Actually, ever since I graduated at the Sarajevo University.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And when did you obtain your engineering degree at Sarajevo University?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And before the war, were you working as a construction engineer?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I also worked at that time as a civil engineer or construction engineer in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And generally speaking, can you give us an idea of the kinds of projects you worked on?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I used to work in a company called Local Authority for Roads and Infrastructure of the Vlasenica Municipality. I worked mostly on the low level construction project and also on building of some facilities and objects. The finance would come from the local authorities. I was the supervisor of the projects, which means that sometimes I had to put some corrections into the plans. And also in that same company that I already mentioned, I would supervise the work of other organs. This is a local authority organ and the abbreviation that we used in B/C/S is SIZ, S-I-Z. That's really the shortest way to explain that part of my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And were you engaged in the army at any time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I served in the JNA in 1977 and 1978.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And where were you based or was this your compulsory service for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was part of my compulsory service.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And then were you mobilised when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: You mean in the early days of the hostilities or latterly?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, when the war broke out, around 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out, I was mobilised and assigned to the Territorial Defence of Vlasenica. Our unit was stationed in hotel Panorama in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we can now turn to 1995, what was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: At the time I held the rank of major, of the reserve force, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what unit were you engaged in?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I was engaged in the 5th Engineers Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And this 5th Engineer Battalion, which corps was it subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It was subordinated to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many people made up the 5th Engineering Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: A bit over a hundred. I can't give you the exact figure. 110, 120, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you -- so that we understand a little bit more about this 5th Engineering Battalion, can you tell us what its function was?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Its task was to serve whatever needs the corps had in terms of engineering works. We received all our orders from the corps and the unit could not be otherwise engaged, if it did not have an order to that effect from its superior command which was that of the Drina Corps. I was charged with construction works within the unit. I was engaged in road works, bridge repairs, development of a passive reflector that was needed for the telecommunications system in Vlasenica. We were also working on the water supply system, and there was also an overhead power line, high voltage power line in Vlasenica, for which we had to develop a project. This is what I was engaged in. However, the unit also dealt with mine clearance, laying minefields, and other activities that were more closely related to the military purpose of the unit. I would also like to add the following. My commander and I divided up the work across the unit in such a way that I was charged with whatever construction works there were, which was my specialty anyhow, and the commander, who was an active serviceman, was occupied with the military activities and activities that I wasn't specifically trained for.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to the unit, and in your reference to the unit, are you talking about the 5th Engineering Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. 5th Engineering Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the unit dealt with mine clearance and laying minefields. Was the battalion also involved in clearing obstacles?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I did mention that. Perhaps it wasn't interpreted. I said that we laid minefields and cleared areas of mines. It depended on the orders given.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What about setting ambushes? Did your battalion -- was your battalion engaged in that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: A battalion -- the battalion was not a combat unit. It was a service-providing unit, which had to serve the needs for engineering work within the corps. The makeup of the unit was such that most of its members came from the profession of builders who, before the war, used to work in various military posts. The majority of them were of an advanced age. That's why we chose to focus predominantly on engineering or construction works for the purposes of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that the battalion was involved in laying of mines. There were members of the 5th Engineering Battalion who had expertise in the laying of mines, is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: You're right. One company, which can only figuratively speaking be called a company, it was called the Company of Pioneers and it numbered some 15 to 20 men. Ten of them were Pioneers, which meant people trained for laying mines and de-mining.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And just returning to the question I asked you before, were any members of this battalion involved in setting ambushes?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: We weren't setting ambushes anywhere outside of our barracks in Konjevic Polje. If you were referring to a document which says that we had been setting ambushes, this meant that we would have more men deployed at night in the stretches between the various guard posts, as well as around the minefields that had been laid around the barracks itself. Outside of the barracks, we didn't have any sort of interventions in terms of setting ambushes or any other military activities. Excuse me, I have to add that we were a small unit, in terms of our strength. We spent most of the time out in the field. Thus, we would secure the barracks by dint of the two minefields on both sides of the road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac and the guard posts which had been designated previously. So, in terms of this sort of activity, we only were charged with providing security to the barracks itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's go back to the formation of the 5th Engineering Battalion. Who was the commander of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Milenko Avramovic was battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what was his rank?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In 1995, what was his rank? Was it Captain First Class?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: In 1995, he was Captain First Class. At a later date, he was given the rank of Major. I don't know when this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you have briefly spoken about his role in the battalion. But can you tell me what his role was as the commander of the battalion? Can you give me a little bit more details on that? What were his duties, his responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, as its commander, he was in command of the battalion. I've already told you that we had, the two of us, divided up the work because he would not have been able to deal with the work-load on his own. He wasn't too happy about attending various construction sites, so he left the entire construction business to me. When I wasn't able to attend to everything because we had some of these sites that were pretty remote, he would give me a hand in checking some of the construction sites that I was unable to go to. And the way we divided up the work was that he would be dealing with the military activities of de-mining and the rest I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was it that commander's duty to know where his units were positioned and what they were engaged in, the materials, the assets of the battalion, was that something that fell within his responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, he was supposed to know. Whenever something was done, it was the result of an order issued by the higher level command. So everybody had to know what was being done at which time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So would the whole battalion be informed of orders that would come from the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No. By no means. Only those who were directly involved. Once an order is issued by the corps, a more detailed order is issued detailing who would be doing what, and then it's copied to the relevant individuals. Once the work is complete, a report is drawn up about it and sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And would your commander know of all the orders coming down from the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if he was aware of all the orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was it his duty to know?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: You know, I was a reserve officer. It wasn't my line of work. I suppose it was his duty, but I don't know what else to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, what was your title or what was your role in the 5th Engineering Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: My title was deputy commander of the 5th Engineering Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And sir, when you were engaged in that role, did you wear a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wore a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If the commander of the 5th Engineering Battalion was not present, would -- who would take over his responsibilities and duties?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, most probably his deputy. If the deputy is absent as well, then the duty officer of the unit would take over.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, sir, when you refer to his deputy, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you have the authority to issue orders to your units within the 5th Engineering Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a power to issue orders independently. The unit could be engaged solely on the basis of an order from the superior command, at least that's what I was told, that there had to be an order on the basis of which an order can be given directly to the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in the absence of your commander, would you be responsible for relaying an order from the Drina Corps command to the appropriate companies or units within the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: If I received an order, it was my duty to implement it, and I could not have done it in any other way but by relaying it to the units that would be appropriate to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, does the name Carina mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Carina?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Carina.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. Do you mean the name or customs?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes: It means customs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: What was the 5th Engineering Battalion's code name in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of communication, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, it changed. I don't know. You've caught me up short there. I think it was one of the code names of the battalion, but it would be the signalmen who would know that. Let me add this: We had a field telephone line, induction lines, as it were, which was out of order for most of the time. It was more out of working order than in working order. Because it was a line that stretched on the ground, and there were frequently times when the lines weren't working.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. The battalion, the 5th Engineering Battalion, where were its headquarters in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Officially, the command of the 5th Engineering Battalion was in Milici, next to a sports field. However, because of shortage of space, we were relocated to Konjevic Polje. It was supposed to be a location solely for the storage of machinery and other assets such -- including supplies. Eventually, a house that had been wrecked was repaired and the command was housed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what type of machinery the 5th Engineering Battalion had?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, we had some old machines. Would you want me to list them all?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: First we had a loader.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the make of it.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It was very old and it needed a lot of repairing before it could be made fully operational. We also had a bulldozer, TG110, which we used for digging up roads where the soil was very hard. It was also an old one, though admittedly a bit better than the loader. But it was the sort of bulldozer that had the lowest strength of the possible bulldozers you could have. We also had a military machine, it was a tractor, KN, that was its designation. It had a loading spoon on the front and a small spoon for -- or a like a backhoe that would be used for digging ditches. Its strength wasn't great but it could be used for small-scale works. Next, we had two small trucks, namely FAPs 13. Furthermore, we had five trailers. They were anyway never used, they were never even switched on. They just were parked there. Maybe they were dredges. We also had some pontoons or rafters, we actually had four rafting points, like -- or actually they were more like river ferries. We had four places, ferry points, but only three rafters, which I don't believe were ever operational, at least during the time I was there, because an embargo was in place between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, and sir, you mentioned that you had a loader, and you noted that the interpreter hadn't picked up the type, which is correct. Could you please tell us what type of loader that was?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: The designation of this loader was ULT. I don't remember the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the ferry points that you mentioned, where were those located?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, they were the pontoon points on Drina, Petrica, Fakovici, Bosansko. Also Sopotnik was in our books as a ferry or pontoon point but there was no pontoon in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that the battalion had certain materials. Can you tell us what materials you had?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any materials, building materials. In the military parlance, materiel, we only used to have explosives and mines.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So the storage that was set up in Konjevic Polje, at the command, that storage contained mines and explosives?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mines, explosives, fuses. It was stored in two buildings that had been rebuilt for that purpose and hence it became warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did you have -- in Konjevic Polje, at the command, did you have offices for the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I already mentioned the fact that we had rebuilt a house into our command. So we had offices and dormitories there. In those other houses where the logistics platoon was situated they used the one building for their own accommodation. This logistics platoon mostly spent its time in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And was the battalion equipped with a kitchen?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, I just told you that the logistics platoon was there, and the kitchen was definitely part of that logistics platoon. It was behind the school. There was a thermo power plant, and we had rebuilt it so that then we had on one side a kitchen and a classroom and on the other side the dining-room and another classroom. We used it as the dining-room.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we have P444 displayed on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you see on this photograph the building where the 5th Engineering Battalion offices were housed?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: You can't see it here. You can't see this building.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was attached to a school. Do you see the school in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No, I can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can we just enlarge that photograph so that we get a closer view of the building?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this intersection?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is the intersection in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And with this enlargement, do you see the school to which the office was attached to?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: The offices were not attached to the school. There was some distance between the school and the offices but I can't see it here, no, not in this photo. That house is not in this photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were any of these buildings used by the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No, no. None of these buildings, the buildings that you can see in this photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, this intersection that you recognise, can you tell me what -- where this road leads to?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I can. But how can I orient you on this picture? I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to simply refer to left and right and maybe it will be enough for you to find your bearings in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's try that.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: So this road here that goes towards the right side of the picture, that's the road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac. And this road with lots of curves, if I may say that, that's the Zvornik-Vlasenica road. Shall I repeat it with the -- with this pencil?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: So this here, this is the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road. And this here, this is the Konjevic Polje-Zvornik road. This part here, that's the road going from Konjevic Polje to Milici and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gajic, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise for the interruption but I have a suggestion. Maybe in order to have a clearer transcript, the witness should actually put some markings on the photo, because this way we are going to be left with a transcript which is not going to be entirely understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right, but in order to do so, we should give the pen to the witness so that he can write on the picture. Mr. Usher, could you please make sure that the witness does have the pen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when I was moving the pencil, I could see it. What, should I do it again? All right. I'll repeat it. This road here that I have just marked, this is the road between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I could briefly interrupt you, could you put perhaps KB to indicate that that's the road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: You mean K-B?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please put K/B with the direction of the arrow. Then we will see towards which direction the road is heading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can you do the same with the other road and tell us where that road leads?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: So using the same system of designation, I'm going to put K-Z, Konjevic Polje-Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And can you -- sorry, were you going to --

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Should I also mark the third segment of the road?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Konjevic Polje-Milici road.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, relative to the -- you said this picture doesn't capture the school which had -- which was used by the battalion or some attachment to it. Can you tell us where that is relative to these roads?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: The building of the elementary school and the place that we used, and I have to emphasise that in that school we only used that one small classroom which was slightly set apart from the rest of the school, it is further away in the direction of Bratunac. I don't know the scale of this photo but approximately from this intersection, the school is about 600 or 700 metres away. That's the first of our facilities, and the last of our facilities on that road is maybe a kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely right, Madam Prosecutor. I was just waiting for the witness to stop talking. So we've reached the end of our hearing today, and we shall resume on Monday, 7th of February, at 9.00. Sir, we haven't finished with your testimony, so we shall resume with you on Monday, and I would like to remind you that you are this Tribunal's witness and therefore you cannot speak about the proceedings with anyone, and you are not -- you cannot speak about it with the Office of the Prosecutor. I would like to thank all the parties, as well as all the people who have assisted us during this hearing. Mr. Registrar, I think that we have to go into private session so that the witness can leave the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, would you like -- do you have anything to tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand that we cannot keep these markings to the next session, so I'd like to tender this now as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is admitted. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This document shall be assigned Exhibit P1766. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Well, I would like to thank once more all the parties and all the people who have helped us in this courtroom and outside the courtroom. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of February 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
